And the genres of books have nine spellings of six genres, so the grouping key is LOWER(TRIM(genre)). Both cleanings are done in the query, the way the data frame code of Data Frames does them in R. The tables are created with DATE columns and the dates are appended as ISO text, so SQLite’s julianday() can compute with them and, with extended_types = TRUE, R still receives Date columns.

source("scenario.R")
library(DBI)
library(dplyr)
#> Attaching package: ‘dplyr’
#>
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’:
#>
#>     filter, lag
#>
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:
#>
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

# Dates are stored as ISO text in DATE columns; extended_types = TRUE hands
# them back to R as Date, and SQL date functions still work on them.
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:", extended_types = TRUE)

dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE books (
    title TEXT, author TEXT, isbn TEXT,
    year INTEGER, genre TEXT, pages INTEGER
  )
")
#> [1] 0
dbAppendTable(con, "books", books)
#> [1] 16

loans_text <- loans
loans_text$loan_date <- format(loans$loan_date)
loans_text$return_date <- format(loans$return_date)
dbExecute(con, "
  CREATE TABLE loans (
    loan_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, isbn TEXT, member TEXT,
    loan_date DATE, return_date DATE
  )
")
#> [1] 0
dbAppendTable(con, "loans", loans_text)
#> [1] 60
str(dbReadTable(con, "loans")[c("loan_date", "return_date")])
#> 'data.frame':	60 obs. of  2 variables:
#>  $ loan_date  : Date, format: "2025-01-14" "2025-01-16" ...
#>  $ return_date: Date, format: "2025-02-04" "2025-01-26" ...

# 1. The question in SQL. The loan period is a parameter, not text.
overdue_sql <- "
  SELECT COALESCE(LOWER(TRIM(b.genre)), 'unknown') AS genre,
         COUNT(*) AS returned,
         SUM(julianday(l.return_date) - julianday(l.loan_date) > ?) AS overdue
  FROM loans AS l
  LEFT JOIN books AS b ON REPLACE(b.isbn, '-', '') = l.isbn
  WHERE l.return_date IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY COALESCE(LOWER(TRIM(b.genre)), 'unknown')
  ORDER BY overdue DESC, genre
"
sql_result <- dbGetQuery(con, overdue_sql, params = list(loan_days))
sql_result
#>             genre returned overdue
#> 1         fiction       19       8
#> 2 science fiction       13       5
#> 3         classic        6       3
#> 4     non-fiction        5       3
#> 5          poetry        5       3
#> 6         mystery        4       2
#> 7         unknown        1       1
colSums(sql_result[c("returned", "overdue")])
#> returned  overdue
#>       53       25

# 2. The same question with dbplyr verbs.
books_key <- tbl(con, "books") |>
  transmute(
    isbn_key = sql("REPLACE(isbn, '-', '')"),
    genre = coalesce(tolower(trimws(genre)), "unknown")
  )
overdue_db <- tbl(con, "loans") |>
  filter(!is.na(return_date)) |>
  left_join(books_key, by = c("isbn" = "isbn_key")) |>
  mutate(
    genre = coalesce(genre, "unknown"),
    held = julianday(return_date) - julianday(loan_date)
  ) |>
  group_by(genre) |>
  summarise(returned = n(), overdue = sum(held > loan_days, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(overdue), genre)
db_result <- collect(overdue_db)
as.data.frame(db_result)
#>             genre returned overdue
#> 1         fiction       19       8
#> 2 science fiction       13       5
#> 3         classic        6       3
#> 4     non-fiction        5       3
#> 5          poetry        5       3
#> 6         mystery        4       2
#> 7         unknown        1       1
isTRUE(all.equal(sql_result, as.data.frame(db_result)))
#> [1] TRUE

# 3. A check in base R, on the data frames that never left R.
books_clean <- data.frame(
  isbn = gsub("-", "", books$isbn),
  genre = tolower(trimws(books$genre))
)
returned <- merge(
  loans[!is.na(loans$return_date), ], books_clean,
  by = "isbn", all.x = TRUE
)
returned$genre[is.na(returned$genre)] <- "unknown"
returned$overdue <- as.integer(returned$return_date - returned$loan_date) >
  loan_days
c(returned = nrow(returned), overdue = sum(returned$overdue, na.rm = TRUE))
#> returned  overdue
#>       53       25
by_genre <- tapply(returned$overdue, returned$genre, sum, na.rm = TRUE)
all(by_genre[sql_result$genre] == sql_result$overdue)
#> [1] TRUE

# Which loan has no matching book? The short ISBN of loan L005.
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT l.loan_id, l.isbn
  FROM loans AS l
  LEFT JOIN books AS b ON REPLACE(b.isbn, '-', '') = l.isbn
  WHERE b.isbn IS NULL
")
#>   loan_id         isbn
#> 1    L005 978030640615

dbDisconnect(con)

Source: DBI package documentation: dbGetQuery

The three results agree. The query keeps the loan period out of the SQL text (> ? with params = list(loan_days)), so the number lives in one place, in the scenario, in R. Of 53 returned loans, 25 are overdue: 8 fiction, 5 science fiction, and 3 each for classic, non-fiction and poetry, 2 for mystery, and 1 with an unknown genre. That last row is the lesson in the join. The loan L005 has a one-digit-short ISBN (978030640615), so no book matches it. An inner JOIN would have dropped the loan, and the total would have been 24 and not 25, with no error to say why. The LEFT JOIN keeps it and gives it the genre unknown, which makes the data problem visible. The last query of the script finds exactly that loan. The scenario’s other deliberate defects behave as they do in R: the loan with the impossible date 2025-02-30 has NULL dates, julianday() of NULL is NULL, the comparison is NULL, and SUM ignores it, so it counts as returned and not overdue; the loan returned before it was borrowed has a negative duration and is not overdue; the 7 unreturned loans are excluded by the WHERE (the question here is about returned loans; for the unreturned, shelf_today takes the place of the return date).

The dbplyr version builds the cleaning step as a lazy table (books_key), joins the loans to it, and ends in the same GROUP BY. sql("REPLACE(isbn, '-', '')") is a SQL fragment that dbplyr does not translate, and everything else is verbs. show_query() on overdue_db would show the nested query it generated.

Other backends in short

  • PostgreSQL (RPostgres): a server database that several people and programs share. The settings come from the environment (PGHOST and the others, or ~/.pgpass), parameters can be written $1, $2, and dbConnect() has timezone and timezone_out arguments for time zones (RPostgres package documentation: Postgres).

  • MariaDB and MySQL (RMariaDB): dbConnect() takes dbname, username, password and host, and can read a MariaDB option file. Its CRAN description says it implements a DBI-compliant interface to MariaDB and MySQL, and the legacy RMySQL package points to it for a modern MySQL client (RMariaDB package documentation: dbConnect).

  • ODBC (odbc): one package for every database with an ODBC driver, from a data source name or a driver and its settings. It is a DBI backend, so everything on this page applies (odbc package documentation: dbConnect).

  • DuckDB (duckdb): an embedded analytical database management system; like SQLite it needs no server. dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb()) keeps the data in RAM, and dbdir names a file (duckdb package documentation: duckdb).

  • Others, such as bigrquery, are listed on the DBI site.

Two newer parts of DBI are named here and not used, because they need packages that are not installed. DBI 1.2.0 (2023-12-20) added a family of Arrow generics (dbGetQueryArrow(), dbSendQueryArrow(), dbFetchArrow(), dbReadTableArrow(), dbWriteTableArrow() and others) with default implementations built on nanoarrow, and the DBI documentation labels these functions experimental (DBI package documentation: dbGetQueryArrow). DBI 1.3.0 added support for OpenTelemetry through the otel and otelsdk packages. For an Arrow-based workflow, the packages that talk Arrow directly are described at https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/ (the arrow package is not installed here and is not run).

Pitfalls

The R FAQ has no entry about databases (a search of the FAQ finds none), so these come from the DBI and RSQLite documentation and from the examples above.

  • Building SQL by pasting values. Use params =, dbQuoteIdentifier() for names and sqlInterpolate() where text is unavoidable. See the section on older tutorials for the output of a pasted query.

  • Forgetting to disconnect, or to clear a result. Close in on.exit(); clear in on.exit(). Both produce a warning in RSQLite and a held server session elsewhere.

  • A vector in params is a loop, not a list of values. Use one placeholder per value for IN.

  • Assuming the types survive. Logical columns return as integers, factors as text and dates as numbers unless extended_types = TRUE and the column is declared DATE.

  • Assuming the order. A table has no order; add ORDER BY when the order matters, including for LIMIT and n =.

  • overwrite = TRUE on the wrong table. It replaces whatever is there.

  • Comparing text with the wrong case or blanks. 'Fiction', 'fiction' and 'Fiction ' are three different values to SQL. Clean at the source or in the query (LOWER(TRIM(x))).

  • Pulling everything and then filtering in R. dbReadTable() followed by a filter reads the whole table. Filter in the query.

  • NA and NULL in comparisons. x = NULL is never true in SQL; use IS NULL. In dbplyr, is.na() becomes IS NULL.

  • Secrets in the script. Environment variables, .Renviron, askpass or keyring; never a literal.

  • Saving a connection. A connection that went through saveRDS() and readRDS() is not valid (dbIsValid() is FALSE, and using it fails with the unhelpful bad_weak_ptr); open a new one in each session (see Serialization: RDS, RData and JSON).

  • Sharing one connection between processes. A worker of a parallel computation should open its own connection (see Parallel and Asynchronous Computing).

Version notes

The entries come from the NEWS files of the packages and from the R NEWS; each package’s NEWS lists its own dates.

Version Change

DBI 0.8 (2018-02-24)

Schema support: Id(), dbListObjects(), dbUnquoteIdentifier(); the new generic dbQuoteLiteral(); dbReadTable() and dbWriteTable() specialise on Id for the table name.

DBI 1.0.0 (2018-05-02)

New generics dbAppendTable(), dbCreateTable(), dbCanConnect(), dbIsReadOnly(); dbListFields() and dbColumnInfo() fully specified.

DBI 1.1.0 (2019-12-15)

dbSendQuery(), dbGetQuery(), dbSendStatement() and dbExecute() gain the immediate argument; examples refer to params instead of param; sqlInterpolate() uses dbQuoteLiteral(); new class DBIConnector.

DBI 1.1.1 (2021-01-04)

dbQuoteLiteral() quotes dates as YYYY-MM-DD without a time zone.

DBI 1.2.0 (2023-12-20)

Arrow generics (dbSendQueryArrow(), dbFetchArrow(), dbGetQueryArrow(), dbReadTableArrow(), dbWriteTableArrow(), dbBindArrow() and others) with default implementations through nanoarrow.

DBI 1.3.0 (2026-02-11)

OpenTelemetry support; dbWithTransaction() calls dbRollback() also on interrupt; many generics are now "nonstandardGeneric".

RSQLite 1.1 (2016-11-25)

Rewritten in C++ with Rcpp; new prepared-query strategy with dbBind(); params in dbGetQuery(), dbSendQuery(), dbExecute() and dbSendStatement() (protects from SQL injection); table names are quoted with dbQuoteIdentifier(); RSQLite no longer attaches DBI when loaded, so write library(DBI).

RSQLite 2.0 (2017-06-18)

64-bit integers returned as integer64 (the bit64 package).

RSQLite 2.1.1 (2018-05-05)

bigint argument of dbConnect().

RSQLite 2.2.3 and 2.2.4 (2021)

extended_types argument of dbConnect(); 2.2.6 (2021-04-11) lets dbDataType() and dbWriteTable() use the extended types.

RSQLite 3.52.0 (2026-05-09)

The version number is aligned with the bundled SQLite version; dbListObjects() for attached databases with a schema prefix.

RSQLite 3.53.2 (2026-06-14)

Optional HTTP/HTTPS virtual file system for read-only remote databases (sqliteRemote() and related functions, documented by RSQLite).

RSQLite 3.53.3 (2026-06-28)

Bundled SQLite 3.53.3. The version checked on this page.

dbplyr 2.5.0 (2024-03-19)

Simpler qualified table names: I("schema_name.table_name"); ident_q() and in_schema() revised.

dbplyr 2.6.0

First-edition backends no longer work; last_sql(); ADBC and JDBC connections; src_memdb() and tbl_memdb() deprecated in favour of memdb(); filter_out() and %notin% (new in R 4.6.0) translated.

R 4.3.0

as.Date(<numeric>) works without origin, which simplifies reading dates stored as numbers.

R 4.6.0

%notin% is new in base R; dbplyr 2.6.0 translates it to NOT IN.

Source: DBI package documentation: NEWS

The dates of the RSQLite and DBI releases are those printed in their NEWS pages (RSQLite package documentation: NEWS, dbplyr package documentation: NEWS); the dbplyr 2.6.0 announcement is on the Posit open source blog (blog material, dbplyr 2.6.0 announcement). The R changes are in R NEWS: Changes in R 4.3.0 and R NEWS: Changes in R 4.6.0. R-devel (the upcoming 4.7.0) is not relevant to this page; DBI and RSQLite release independently of R.

Where older tutorials differ

The R Data Import/Export manual’s chapter on relational databases is the official text, and parts of it describe the state of DBI when it was written. Its example uses the RMySQL package, dbDriver("MySQL"), a query built with paste(), and fetch(); it maps data frame row names to a row_names field; and it describes the DBI front-end as a proposal. The RMySQL package’s own CRAN description now calls it a legacy DBI interface and points to RMariaDB for a modern MySQL client. Many blog posts and answers follow the manual, so the patterns recur. The script below shows the one that matters most with real output, and it is the contrast the rest of the page is built on.

A pasted query, and the same function with a parameter

source("scenario.R")
library(DBI)

# The R Data Import/Export manual still shows a driver chosen by name. In a
# session where the backend package has not been loaded, that fails ...
tryCatch(dbDriver("SQLite"), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "Couldn't find driver SQLite. Looked in:\n* global namespace\n* in package called SQLite\n* in package called RSQLite"

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
dbWriteTable(con, "books", books, row.names = FALSE)

# An older tutorial pastes the user's text into the SQL. Do not copy this.
find_by_genre_unsafe <- function(con, genre) {
  sql <- paste0("SELECT title FROM books WHERE genre = '", genre, "'")
  dbGetQuery(con, sql)
}
find_by_genre_unsafe(con, "Poetry")
#>                   title
#> 1 Garden of Small Fires
#> 2           Paper Moons

# A name with an apostrophe breaks the query ...
tryCatch(
  find_by_genre_unsafe(con, "O'Brien"),
  error = \(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
#> [1] "near \"Brien\": syntax error"

# ... and a crafted value changes what the query means: every book comes back.
nrow(find_by_genre_unsafe(con, "x' OR '1'='1"))
#> [1] 16

# RSQLite runs only the first statement of a string, which stops a stacked
# DROP TABLE here; that is a property of this backend, not a defence.
tryCatch(
  find_by_genre_unsafe(con, "x'; DROP TABLE books; --"),
  warning = \(w) conditionMessage(w)
)
#> [1] "Ignoring remaining part of query: DROP TABLE books; --'"
dbListTables(con)
#> [1] "books"

# The same function with a parameter: the value is never part of the SQL.
find_by_genre <- function(con, genre) {
  dbGetQuery(
    con, "SELECT title FROM books WHERE genre = ?",
    params = list(genre)
  )
}
find_by_genre(con, "Poetry")
#>                   title
#> 1 Garden of Small Fires
#> 2           Paper Moons
nrow(find_by_genre(con, "x' OR '1'='1"))
#> [1] 0
nrow(find_by_genre(con, "O'Brien"))
#> [1] 0

# ... and works once RSQLite is loaded, as the line above has just done.
dbDriver("SQLite")
#> <SQLiteDriver>

# fetch() is the pre-DBI name of dbFetch().
res <- dbSendQuery(con, "SELECT title FROM books ORDER BY title")
fetch(res, n = 2)
#>                  title
#> 1   the quiet streets
#> 2        A Map of Salt
dbClearResult(res)

dbDisconnect(con)

Source: DBI package documentation: Advanced DBI usage

The first function builds the SQL by pasting genre between quotation marks, which is what the manual’s paste("select row_names, Murder from arrests", "where Rape > 30 ...") pattern becomes when one value is variable. It works for "Poetry". A value with an apostrophe breaks it (near "Brien": syntax error), which is the harmless way this fails. A value that closes the string and continues the logic (x' OR '1'='1) makes the WHERE true for every row: all 16 books came back for a genre that does not exist. That is SQL injection: the person who supplies the value rewrote the query. RSQLite stopped the third attempt, the stacked DROP TABLE, only because it runs a single statement per call and warned about the rest (Ignoring remaining part of query: ...); that is not protection, and a backend that executes every statement in the string would not have stopped it. The rewritten function with params = list(genre) returns the two poetry books for "Poetry" and nothing for the other two values, because they are only text to compare with. sprintf() has the same problem as paste() when the format has a %s; sprintf("... %d", n) with a number is safe only because %d will not accept text.

The last lines of the script are two other habits from the manual’s era. dbDriver("SQLite") chooses the driver by name; it fails, in a session where RSQLite has not been loaded, with Couldn't find driver SQLite, followed by the places it looked, and works after the package is loaded. fetch() is the name the older DBI used for what is now dbFetch(); RSQLite still exports it.

Other things that changed

Older tutorial writes Current practice Why Since

dbGetQuery(con, paste0("... WHERE x = '", v, "'")) or sprintf()

dbGetQuery(con, "... WHERE x = ?", params = list(v))

A parameter is data and never SQL; see the output above.

RSQLite 1.1 (2016)

dbDriver("MySQL") with RMySQL, dbDriver("PostgreSQL") with RPostgreSQL

dbConnect(RMariaDB::MariaDB(), ...), dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), ...)

RMySQL’s CRAN description calls it a legacy DBI interface and points to RMariaDB; RPostgres describes itself as a fully DBI-compliant C++-backed interface. The older packages are still on CRAN.

n/a

library(RSQLite) to get DBI’s functions

library(DBI), then dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ...)

RSQLite no longer attaches DBI when loaded.

RSQLite 1.1 (2016)

dbSendQuery() for INSERT and UPDATE

dbExecute(), or dbSendStatement() for reuse

They return the number of rows affected and release the result.

DBI 0.5

fetch(res)

dbFetch(res)

dbFetch() is the generic in the DBI reference; fetch() is not listed there, though RSQLite still exports it.

n/a

dbSendPreparedQuery() and dbGetPreparedQuery()

dbSendQuery() with dbBind(), or params =

RSQLite’s NEWS calls the old functions never part of the official API, reimplemented with a deprecation warning.

RSQLite 1.1 (2016)

dbWriteTable(con, "t", df) expecting row names to be kept

row.names = TRUE when wanted; otherwise a column

DBI leaves row names out by default (see the output in the section on tables).

n/a

as.Date(x, origin = "1970-01-01") for dates stored as numbers

as.Date(x), or extended_types = TRUE and DATE columns

R accepts a numeric argument; RSQLite reads declared DATE columns as Date.

R 4.3.0; RSQLite 2.2.x

RODBC::odbcConnect() and sqlQuery()

dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), dsn = ...) and the DBI functions

RODBC has its own function set; odbc is a DBI backend, so it works with dbplyr and the code on this page. RODBC, described in the manual, is still on CRAN.

odbc package

sqldf::sqldf("select ...") on a data frame

A DBI connection (dbWriteTable() then dbGetQuery()), or dplyr or data.table directly on the frame

sqldf creates a database behind the scenes, copies the data frames into it, runs the query and returns the result; DBI shows each step. sqldf is still on CRAN.

n/a

src_memdb() and tbl_memdb()

tbl(con, "table") on a DBI connection, or dbplyr::memdb() for a throw-away database

dbplyr 2.6.0 deprecates src_memdb() and tbl_memdb().

dbplyr 2.6.0

A password written in the script

Sys.getenv(), .Renviron, askpass or keyring

A literal ends up in version control.

always

dbListConnections() to find forgotten connections

on.exit(dbDisconnect(con)) where the connection is made

There is no method for RSQLite in 3.53.3; the connection is closed by the code that opened it.

always
